Computing Multi-Eigenpairs of High-Dimensional Eigenvalue Problems Using Tensor Neural Networks

This work was supported in part by the National Key Research and Development Program of China (2019YFA0709601), the National Center for Mathematics and Interdisciplinary Science, CAS.
Yifan Wang Note: LSEC, NCMIS, Institute of Computational Mathematics, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China, and School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China (wangyifan@lsec.cc.ac.cn).    Hehu Xie Note: LSEC, NCMIS, Institute of Computational Mathematics, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China, and School of Mathematical Sciences, University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100049, China (hhxie@lsec.cc.ac.cn).
Abstract

In this paper, we propose a type of tensor-neural-network-based machine learning method to compute multi-eigenpairs of high dimensional eigenvalue problems without Monte-Carlo procedure. Solving multi-eigenvalues and their corresponding eigenfunctions is one of the basic tasks in mathematical and computational physics. With the help of tensor neural network and deep Ritz method, the high dimensional integrations included in the loss functions of the machine learning process can be computed with high accuracy. The high accuracy of high dimensional integrations can improve the accuracy of the machine learning method for computing multi-eigenpairs of high dimensional eigenvalue problems. Here, we introduce the tensor neural network and design the machine learning method for computing multi-eigenpairs of the high dimensional eigenvalue problems. The proposed numerical method is validated with plenty of numerical examples.

Keywords. high-dimensional eigenvalue problem, tensor neural network, deep Ritz method, high-accuracy, machine learning, multi-eigenpairs.

AMS subject classifications. 65N30, 65N25, 65L15, 65B99

1 Introduction

In modern sciences and engineers, there exist many high-dimensional problems, which arise from quantum mechanics, statistical mechanics, and financial engineer. There have appeared more and more high dimensional eigenvalue problems along with the developments of science and engineer. Computing the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of high dimensional operators becomes more and more important in modern scientific computing. The most famous and important high dimensional eigenvalue problem is the Schrödinger equation from quantum mechanics. The classical numerical methods, such as finite difference, finite element, spectral, can only solve the low dimensional Schrödinger equations for some simple systems. Using these classical numerical methods to solve high dimensional eigenvalue problems will suffer from the so-called curse of dimensionality since the number of degrees of freedom and computational complexity grows exponentially as the dimension increases.

For the high dimensional problems, the Monte-Carlo based methods attract more and more attentions since it provides the possibility to solve high dimensional problems in the stochastic sense. For example, there are two well known variational Monte Carlo (VMC) [6] and diffusion Monte Carlo (DMC) [27] methods for high-dimensional eigenvalue problems in quantum mechanics. Recently, many numerical methods based on machine learning have been proposed to solve the high-dimensional PDEs ([3, 8, 9, 13, 14, 23, 24, 25, 26, 28, 30, 35, 36]). Among these machine learning methods, neural network-based methods attract more and more attention since it can be used to build approximations to the exact solutions of PDEs by machine learning methods. The essential reason is that neural networks can approximate any function given enough parameters. This type of method also provides a possible way to solve many useful high-dimensional PDEs from physics, chemistry, biology, engineering, and so on.

Due to its universal approximation property, the fully-connected neural network (FNN) is the most widely used architecture to build the functions for solving high-dimensional PDEs. There are several types of FNN-based methods such as the well-known deep Ritz [9], deep Galerkin method [30], PINN [28], and weak adversarial networks [35] for solving high-dimensional PDEs by designing different loss functions. Among these methods, the loss functions always include computing high-dimensional integration for the functions defined by FNN. For example, the loss functions of the deep Ritz method require computing the integrations on the high-dimensional domain for the functions which is constructed by FNN. Direct numerical integration for the high-dimensional functions also meets the “curse of dimensionality”. Always, the Monte-Carlo method is adopted to do the high-dimensional integration with some types of sampling methods [9, 15]. Due to the low convergence rate of the Monte-Carlo method, the solutions obtained by the FNN-based numerical methods are difficult to obtain high accuracy and stable convergence process. In other words, the Monte-Carlo method decreases computational work in each forward propagation by decreasing the simulation efficiency and stability of the FNN-based numerical methods for solving high-dimensional PDEs.

In [32], based on the deep Ritz method, a type of tensor neural network (TNN) is proposed to build the trial functions for solving high-dimensional PDEs. The TNN is a function being designed by the tensor product operations on the neural networks or by correlated low-rank CANDECOMP/PARAFAC (CP) tensor decomposition [17, 22] approximations of FNNs. An important advantage is that we do not need to use Monte-Carlo method to do the integration for the functions which is constructed by TNN. The high dimensional integration of the TNN functions can be decomposed into one-dimensional integrations which can be computed by the highly accurate Gauss type quadrature scheme. The computational work for the integration of the functions by TNN is only a polynomial scale of the dimension, which means the TNN overcomes the “curse of dimensionality” in some sense for solving high-dimensional PDEs. Furthermore, the high accuracy of high dimensional integration can improve the TNN-based machine learning methods for solving high-dimensional problems. The TNN-based machine learning methods have already been used to solve the smallest eigenvalue and its corresponding eigenfunction of high-dimensional eigenvalue problems [32] and Schrödinger equations in [33].

In this paper, we investigate the applications of TNN for computing multi-eigenpairs of high dimensional eigenvalue problems. The aim of this paper is to propose a universal machine learning solver for computing multi-eigenpairs of high dimensional eigenvalue problems based on the TNN and deep Ritz method without the a priori knowledge of the actual or guessed solutions. Furthermore, the proposed eigensolver can compute multi-eigenpairs of the high dimensional eigenvalue problem with obviously better accuracy than the Montor-Carlo based machine learning methods. In this paper, we will also find that the applications of TNN and the high accuracy of high dimensional integrations bring more choices to define the loss functions for the machine learning methods. For example, the loss function in this paper for computing multi-eigenpairs is more like the classical way for computing eigenvalue problems. The proposed eigensolver provides a new way to solve high dimensional eigenvalue problems from physics, chemistry, biology, engineering, and so on. We will provide plenty of numerical results for the examples from the physics and material sciences.

An outline of the paper goes as follows. In Section 2, we introduce the TNN architecture and its approximation property. In Section 3, the TNN-based machine learning method and corresponding numerical integration schemes are introduced for solving multi-eigenpairs of the high dimensional eigenvalue problems. Section 4 is devoted to providing numerical examples to validate the accuracy and efficiency of the proposed numerical methods. Finally, some concluding remarks are given in the last section.

2 Tensor neural network architecture

TNN structure, its approximation property and the computational complexity of related integration have been discussed and investigated in [32]. In this section, we introduce the architecture of TNN. In order to express clearly and facilitate the construction of the TNN method for solving multi-eigenpairs of high dimensional eigenvalue problems, here, we will also elaborate on some important definitions and properties.

TNN is a neural network of low-rank structure, which is built by the tensor product of of several one-dimensional input and multidimensional output subnetworks. Due to the low-rank structure of TNN, an efficient and accurate quadrature scheme can be designed for the TNN-related high dimensional integrations such as the inner product of two TNNs. In [32], we introduce TNN in detail and propose its numerical integration scheme with the polynomial scale computational complexity of the dimension. For each i=1,2,⋯,di=1,2,\cdots,d, we use Φi​(xi,θi)=(ϕi,1​(xi,θi),ϕi,2​(xi,θi),⋯,ϕi,p​(xi,θi))\Phi_{i}(x_{i};\theta_{i})=(\phi_{i,1}(x_{i};\theta_{i}),\phi_{i,2}(x_{i};\theta_{i}),\cdots,\phi_{i,p}(x_{i};\theta_{i})) to denote a subnetwork that maps a set Ωi⊂ℝ\Omega_{i}\subset\mathbb{R} to ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}, where Ωi,i=1,⋯,d,\Omega_{i},i=1,\cdots,d, can be a bounded interval (ai,bi)(a_{i},b_{i}), the whole line (−∞,+∞)(-\infty,+\infty) or the half line (ai,+∞)(a_{i},+\infty). The number of layers and neurons in each layer, the selections of activation functions and other hyperparameters can be different in different subnetworks. In this paper, in order to improve the numerical stability further, the TNN is defined as follows:

Ψ(x;Θ)=∑j=1pcjϕ^1,j(x1;θ1)ϕ^2,j(x2;θ2)⋯ϕ^d,j(xd;θd)=∑j=1pcj∏i=1dϕ^i,j(xi;θi),\displaystyle\Psi(x;\Theta)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}c_{j}\widehat{\phi}_{1,j}(x_{1};\theta_{1})\widehat{\phi}_{2,j}(x_{2};\theta_{2})\cdots\widehat{\phi}_{d,j}(x_{d};\theta_{d})=\sum_{j=1}^{p}c_{j}\prod_{i=1}^{d}\widehat{\phi}_{i,j}(x_{i};\theta_{i}), (2.1)

where c={cj}j=1pc=\{c_{j}\}_{j=1}^{p} is a set of trainable parameters, Θ={c,θ1,⋯,θd}\Theta=\{c,\theta_{1},\cdots,\theta_{d}\} denotes all parameters of the whole architecture. For i=1,⋯,d,j=1,⋯,pi=1,\cdots,d,j=1,\cdots,p, ϕ^i,j​(xi,θi)\widehat{\phi}_{i,j}(x_{i},\theta_{i}) is a normalized functions as follows:

ϕ^i,j​(xi,θi)=ϕi,j​(xi,θi)‖ϕi,j​(xi,θi)‖L2​(Ωi).\displaystyle\widehat{\phi}_{i,j}(x_{i},\theta_{i})=\frac{\phi_{i,j}(x_{i},\theta_{i})}{\|\phi_{i,j}(x_{i},\theta_{i})\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{i})}}. (2.2)

In Section 3.2, we will discuss the architectures for each subnetwork Φi​(xi,θi)\Phi_{i}(x_{i};\theta_{i}) in detail according to different types of Ωi\Omega_{i}. The TNN architecture (2.1) and the one defined in [32] are mathematically equivalent, but (2.1) has better numerical stability during the training process. Figure 1 shows the corresponding architecture of TNN. From Figure 1 and numerical tests, we can find the parameters for each rank of TNN are correlated by the FNN, which guarantee the stability of the TNN-based machine learning methods. This is also an important difference from the tensor finite element methods.

In order to show the reasonableness of TNN, we now introduce the approximation property from [32]. Since there exists the isomorphism relation between Hm(Ω1×⋯×Ωd)H^{m}(\Omega_{1}\times\cdots\times\Omega_{d}) and the tensor product space Hm(Ω1)⊗⋯⊗Hm(Ωd)H^{m}(\Omega_{1})\otimes\cdots\otimes H^{m}(\Omega_{d}), the process of approximating the function f(x)∈Hm(Ω1×⋯×Ωd)f(x)\in H^{m}(\Omega_{1}\times\cdots\times\Omega_{d}) by the TNN defined as (2.1) can be regarded as searching for a correlated CP decomposition structure to approximate f⁡(x)f(x) in the space Hm(Ω1)⊗⋯⊗Hm(Ωd)H^{m}(\Omega_{1})\otimes\cdots\otimes H^{m}(\Omega_{d}) with the rank being not greater than pp. In [32] we introduce and prove the following approximation result to the functions in the space Hm(Ω1×⋯×Ωd)H^{m}(\Omega_{1}\times\cdots\times\Omega_{d}) under the sense of HmH^{m}-norm.

Theorem 1.

Assume that each Ωi\Omega_{i} is an interval in ℝ\mathbb{R} for i=1,⋯,di=1,\cdots,d, Ω=Ω1×⋯×Ωd\Omega=\Omega_{1}\times\cdots\times\Omega_{d}, and the function f​(x)∈Hm​(Ω)f(x)\in H^{m}(\Omega). Then for any tolerance ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exist a positive integer pp and the corresponding TNN defined by (2.1) such that the following approximation property holds

‖f⁡(x)−Ψ⁡(x,θ)‖Hm​(Ω)<ε.\|f(x)-\Psi(x;\theta)\|_{H^{m}(\Omega)}<\varepsilon. (2.3)

The motivation for employing the TNN architectures is to provide high accuracy and high efficiency in calculating variational forms of high-dimensional problems in which high-dimensional integrations are included. The TNN itself can approximate functions in Sobolev space with respect to HmH^{m}-norm. Therefore we naturally put forward an approach to solve high-dimensional PDEs and the ground state eigenpair in [32, 33]. The major contribution of this paper is to propose a TNN-based machine learning method to compute the leading multi-eigenpairs of high-dimensional eigenvalue problems. We will find that the designing of the machine learning method in this paper for computing multi-eigenpairs also shows the advantages of TNN.

3 Machine learning method for computing multi-eigenpairs

This section is devoted to introducing the TNN-based machine learning method [11] to compute the multi-eigenpairs of high dimensional eigenvalue problems. We will introduce the way to build the eigenfunction approximations by TNN functions and the quadrature schemes to compute the inner products of the TNN functions.

3.1 Approximate eigen-subspace by TNNs

In this subsection, we present the TNN-based discretization of eigenvalue problems for solving multi-eigenpairs. Briefly speaking, analogous to the subspace projection method such as the finite element method, instead of using the finite element basis, our approach uses several TNNs as the basis to span a subspace of solution space and restrict the problem into this finite dimensional subspace. Through a machine learning process, an optimal approximation of the eigen-subspace represented by TNNs will be found. Then the final multi-eigenpair approximations are obtained by solving a finite-dimensional matrix eigenvalue problem, which is similar to the Rayleigh-Ritz step in the classical eigensolvers for the matrix eigenvalue problems [29].

For generality, we describe the eigenvalue and the TNN-based machine learning method in the abstract way. More specifically, assume Sobolev spaces 𝒱\mathcal{V} and 𝒲\mathcal{W} are two Hilbert spaces and satisfy 𝒱⊂𝒲\mathcal{V}\subset\mathcal{W}. And let a⁡(⋅,⋅)a(\cdot,\cdot) and b⁡(⋅,⋅)b(\cdot,\cdot) denote two positive definite symmetric bilinear forms on 𝒱×𝒱\mathcal{V}\times\mathcal{V} and 𝒲×𝒲\mathcal{W}\times\mathcal{W}, respectively. Furthermore, based on these bilinear forms, we can define the norms on the space 𝒱\mathcal{V} and 𝒲\mathcal{W} as follows

‖v‖a\displaystyle\|v\|_{a} =\displaystyle= a⁡(v,v),∀v∈𝒱,\displaystyle\sqrt{a(v,v)},\ \ \ \forall v\in\mathcal{V}, (3.1)
‖w‖b\displaystyle\|w\|_{b} =\displaystyle= b⁡(w,w),∀w∈𝒲.\displaystyle\sqrt{b(w,w)},\ \ \ \forall w\in\mathcal{W}. (3.2)

Assume the norm ∥⋅∥a\|\cdot\|_{a} is relatively compact with respect to the norm ∥⋅∥b\|\cdot\|_{b} [7].

To describe our method and to build the loss function for computing leading kk eigenpairs briefly, we focus on the following general eigenvalue problem: Find (λ,u)∈ℝ×𝒱(\lambda,u)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathcal{V} such that b⁡(u,u)=1b(u,u)=1 and

a⁡(u,v)=λ​b​(u,v),∀v∈𝒱.\displaystyle a(u,v)=\lambda b(u,v),\ \ \ \forall v\in\mathcal{V}. (3.3)

It is well known that the eigenvalue problem (3.3) has an eigenvalue sequence {λj}\{\lambda_{j}\} (cf. [2]):

0<λ1≤λ2≤⋯≤λk≤⋯,limk→∞λk=∞,0<\lambda_{1}\leq\lambda_{2}\leq\cdots\leq\lambda_{k}\leq\cdots,\ \ \ \lim_{k\rightarrow\infty}\lambda_{k}=\infty,

and associated eigenfunctions

u1,u2,⋯,uk,⋯,u_{1},u_{2},\cdots,u_{k},\cdots,

where b⁡(ui,uj)=δi​jb(u_{i},u_{j})=\delta_{ij} (δi​j\delta_{ij} denotes the Kronecker function). In the sequence {λj}\{\lambda_{j}\}, the λj\lambda_{j} are repeated according to their geometric multiplicity.

The eigenvalues satisfy the minimum-maximum principle [2]

λk=min𝒱k⊂𝒱dim𝒱k=k⁡maxf∈𝒱k⁡ℛ⁡(f)=maxf∈span⁡{u1,⋯,uk}⁡ℛ⁡(f),\displaystyle\lambda_{k}=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{V}_{k}\subset\mathcal{V}\\ \dim\mathcal{V}_{k}=k\end{subarray}}\max_{f\in\mathcal{V}_{k}}\mathcal{R}(f)=\max_{f\in{\rm span}\{u_{1},\cdots,u_{k}\}}\mathcal{R}(f), (3.4)

where ℛ⁡(f)=a⁡(f,f)/b⁡(f,f)\mathcal{R}(f)=a(f,f)/b(f,f) denotes the Rayleigh quotient of the function ff. Let us define 𝒱k=span⁡{v1,⋯,vk}\mathcal{V}_{k}={\rm span}\{v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}\} and vi∈𝒱v_{i}\in\mathcal{V} for i=1,⋯,ki=1,\cdots,k are linearly independent of each other. Furthermore, we also define 𝒰k=span⁡{u1,⋯,uk}\mathcal{U}_{k}={\rm span}\{u_{1},\cdots,u_{k}\} which denotes the eigensubspace with respect to the leading kk eigenvalues. Use the terminology of the subspace approximation to the eigenvalue problems, we define the stiffness matrix 𝒜⁡(v1,⋯,vk)\mathcal{A}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}) and mass matrix ℬ⁡(v1,⋯,vk)\mathcal{B}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}) as follows

𝒜⁡(v1,⋯,vk)=(𝒜i​j​(v1,⋯,vk))1≤i,j≤k=(a⁡(vi,vj))1≤i,j≤k∈ℝk×k,\displaystyle\mathcal{A}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k})=\Big(\mathcal{A}_{ij}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k})\Big)_{1\leq i,j\leq k}=\Big(a(v_{i},v_{j})\Big)_{1\leq i,j\leq k}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}, (3.5)
ℬ⁡(v1,⋯,vk)=(ℬi​j​(v1,⋯,vk))1≤i,j≤k=(b⁡(vi,vj))1≤i,j≤k∈ℝk×k.\displaystyle\mathcal{B}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k})=\Big(\mathcal{B}_{ij}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k})\Big)_{1\leq i,j\leq k}=\Big(b(v_{i},v_{j})\Big)_{1\leq i,j\leq k}\in\mathbb{R}^{k\times k}. (3.6)

Then due to the minimum-maximum principle, by simple derivation, the summation of the leading kk eigenvalues satisfies the following optimization problem

∑i=1kλi=min𝒱k=span{v1⋯,vk}vj∈𝒱,j=1,⋯,k⁡trace⁡(ℬ−1​(v1,⋯,vk)​𝒜​(v1,⋯,vk)),\displaystyle\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_{i}=\min_{\begin{subarray}{c}\mathcal{V}_{k}={\rm span}\{v_{1}\cdots,v_{k}\}\\ v_{j}\in\mathcal{V},j=1,\cdots,k\end{subarray}}{\rm trace}\left(\mathcal{B}^{-1}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k})\mathcal{A}(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k})\right), (3.7)

and the eigensubspace with respect to the leading kk eigenvalues consists with

𝒰k=span{u1,⋯,uk}=argmin𝒱k=span{v1⋯,vk}⊂𝒱trace(ℬ−1(v1,⋯,vk)𝒜(v1,⋯,vk)).\displaystyle\mathcal{U}_{k}={\rm span}\{u_{1},\cdots,u_{k}\}=\arg\min_{\mathcal{V}_{k}={\rm span}\{v_{1}\cdots,v_{k}\}\subset\mathcal{V}}{\rm trace}\Big(\mathcal{B}^{-1}\big(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}\big)\mathcal{A}\big(v_{1},\cdots,v_{k}\big)\Big). (3.8)

We approximate 𝒰k\mathcal{U}_{k} by a space spanned by kk TNNs Ψ1​(x,Θ1)\Psi_{1}(x;\Theta_{1}), ⋯\cdots, Ψk​(x,Θk)\Psi_{k}(x;\Theta_{k}), where each Ψℓ​(x,Θℓ)\Psi_{\ell}(x;\Theta_{\ell}) is defined by (2.1) with Φi,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ)=(ϕi,1,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ)CLOSE\Phi_{i,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})=(\phi_{i,1,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}), ϕi,2,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ)\phi_{i,2,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}), ⋯\cdots, OPENϕi,p,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ))\phi_{i,p,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})) as the ii-th subnetwork of the ℓ\ell-th TNN. Then, for ℓ=1,⋯,k\ell=1,\cdots,k, the ℓ\ell-th TNN Ψℓ​(x,Θℓ)\Psi_{\ell}(x;\Theta_{\ell}) is denoted as

Ψℓ​(x,Θℓ)=∑j=1pℓcj,ℓ​∏i=1dϕ^i,j,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ),\displaystyle\Psi_{\ell}(x;\Theta_{\ell})=\sum_{j=1}^{p_{\ell}}c_{j,\ell}\prod_{i=1}^{d}\widehat{\phi}_{i,j,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}), (3.9)

where each cℓ={cj,ℓ}j=1pc_{\ell}=\{c_{j,\ell}\}_{j=1}^{p} is a set of trainable parameters, each Θℓ={cℓ,θ1,ℓ,⋯,θd,ℓ}\Theta_{\ell}=\{c_{\ell},\theta_{1,\ell},\cdots,\theta_{d,\ell}\} denotes all parameters of the ℓ\ell-th TNN. Similar to (2.2), each ϕ^i,j,ℓ\widehat{\phi}_{i,j,\ell} is normalized function. We can select the appropriate activation function such that all Ψℓ​(x,Θℓ),ℓ=1,⋯,k\Psi_{\ell}(x;\Theta_{\ell}),\ell=1,\cdots,k belong to the space 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Let us define p=max⁡{p1,⋯,pk}p=\max\{p_{1},\cdots,p_{k}\}. These kk TNNs are trained using the following loss function

Loss⁡(Ψ1​(x,Θ1),⋯,Ψk​(x,Θk))\displaystyle{\rm Loss}\Big(\Psi_{1}(x;\Theta_{1}),\cdots,\Psi_{k}(x;\Theta_{k})\Big)
=trace⁡(ℬ−1​(Ψ1​(x,Θ1),⋯,Ψk​(x,Θk))​𝒜​(Ψ1​(x,Θ1),⋯,Ψk​(x,Θk))).\displaystyle={\rm trace}\Big(\mathcal{B}^{-1}\big(\Psi_{1}(x;\Theta_{1}),\cdots,\Psi_{k}(x;\Theta_{k})\big)\mathcal{A}\big(\Psi_{1}(x;\Theta_{1}),\cdots,\Psi_{k}(x;\Theta_{k})\big)\Big). (3.10)

Since we do the inner-products of TNN in (3.10), the way to build the loss function is deep Ritz type. In order to assemble the matrices 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} in (3.10), we need to compute the high dimensional integrations included in the bilinear forms a⁡(⋅,⋅)a(\cdot,\cdot) and b⁡(⋅,⋅)b(\cdot,\cdot) in (3.3). The detailed method for assembling the matrices 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} in (3.10) will be introduced in Section 3.2. The loss function (3.10) is automatically differentiable thanks to packages that support backpropagation such as TensorFlow and PyTorch. In this paper, the gradient descent (GD) method is adopted to update all trainable parameters

Θℓ−η∇ΘℓLoss→Θℓ,ℓ=1,⋯,k,\displaystyle\Theta_{\ell}-\eta\nabla_{\Theta_{\ell}}{\rm Loss}\rightarrow\Theta_{\ell},\ \ \ \ell=1,\cdots,k, (3.11)

where η\eta is the learning rate and adjusted by the ADAM optimizer [20].

After sufficient training steps, we obtain a sequence of parameters {Θ1∗,⋯,Θk∗}\{\Theta_{1}^{*},\cdots,\Theta_{k}^{*}\} such that the loss function (3.10) arrives its minimum value under the required tolerance. By solving the following finite-dimensional matrix eigenvalue problem

𝒜⁡(Ψ1​(x,Θ1∗),⋯,Ψk​(x,Θk∗))​𝐲=λ​ℬ​(Ψ1​(x,Θ1∗),⋯,Ψk​(x,Θk∗))​𝐲,\displaystyle\mathcal{A}\big(\Psi_{1}(x;\Theta_{1}^{*}),\cdots,\Psi_{k}(x;\Theta_{k}^{*})\big)\mathbf{y}=\lambda\mathcal{B}\big(\Psi_{1}(x;\Theta_{1}^{*}),\cdots,\Psi_{k}(x;\Theta_{k}^{*})\big)\mathbf{y}, (3.12)

we obtain a sequence of eigenvalues

0<λ^1≤λ^2≤⋯≤λ^k\displaystyle 0<\widehat{\lambda}_{1}\leq\widehat{\lambda}_{2}\leq\cdots\leq\widehat{\lambda}_{k}\, (3.13)

and corresponding eigenvectors

𝐲1,𝐲2,⋯,𝐲k,\displaystyle\mathbf{y}_{1},\mathbf{y}_{2},\cdots,\mathbf{y}_{k}, (3.14)

where 𝐲j=[yj,1,⋯,yj,k]⊤\mathbf{y}_{j}=[y_{j,1},\cdots,y_{j,k}]^{\top} for j=1,⋯,kj=1,\cdots,k. Then λ^1\widehat{\lambda}_{1}, ⋯\cdots, λ^k\widehat{\lambda}_{k} can be chosen as the approximations to the first kk eigenvalues λ1\lambda_{1}, ⋯\cdots, λk\lambda_{k} and the corresponding approximations u^1\widehat{u}_{1}, ⋯\cdots, u^k\widehat{u}_{k} to the first kk eigenfunctions of problem (3.3) can be obtained by the following linear combination procedure

u^j​(x)\displaystyle\widehat{u}_{j}(x) =\displaystyle= ∑ℓ=1kyj,ℓ​Ψℓ​(x,Θℓ∗).\displaystyle\sum_{\ell=1}^{k}y_{j,\ell}\Psi_{\ell}(x;\Theta_{\ell}^{*}). (3.15)
Remark 1.

In [36], the loss function is defined by the summation of kk Rayleigh quotients and a penalty term which constrains the kk neural networks to be mutually orthogonal and normalized. Different form [36], in this paper, the loss function (3.10) is defined without the penalty term and the orthogonalization condition of kk TNNs is not imposed directly. The reason is that the use of TNN architectures can provide a high-accuracy and high-efficiency quadrature scheme, as we will see in Section 3.2, for assembling the matrices in the loss function (3.10) and eigenvalue problem (3.12). The penalty term makes optimization process much more difficult and thus affects the final accuracy. The orthogonalization condition is implicitly guaranteed by solving the optimization problem in the machine learning method with the loss function (3.10). The main innovation of the present paper is for the first time to apply the TNN architecture to compute multi-eigenpairs of high dimensional eigenvalue problems with high accuracy. In Section 4.1, we will give an example from [36] to show the advantages of proposed approach.

3.2 Quadrature scheme for inner product

In this subsection, we provide a detailed description to calculate inner products in the loss function (3.10). For simplicity, we are concerned with the following model problem as an example: Find (λ,u)∈ℝ×H01​(Ω)(\lambda,u)\in\mathbb{R}\times H_{0}^{1}(\Omega) such that

{−Δ​u+V⁡(x)​u=λ​u,inΩ,u=0,on​∂Ω,\left\{\begin{aligned} -\Delta u+V(x)u&=\lambda u,&&\text{in}\ \ \Omega,\\ u&=0,&&\text{on}\ \partial\Omega,\end{aligned}\right. (3.16)

where Ω=Ω1×⋯×Ωd\Omega=\Omega_{1}\times\cdots\times\Omega_{d}, each Ωi,i=1,⋯,d,\Omega_{i},i=1,\cdots,d, can be a bounded interval (ai,bi)(a_{i},b_{i}), the whole line (−∞,+∞)(-\infty,+\infty) or the half line (ai,+∞)(a_{i},+\infty), V​(x)∈L2​(Ω)V(x)\in L^{2}(\Omega) is a potential function. We assume that the potential V⁡(x)V(x) has separated representation in the tensor product space L2(Ω1)⊗⋯⊗L2(Ωd)L^{2}(\Omega_{1})\otimes\cdots\otimes L^{2}(\Omega_{d}) as follows

V⁡(x)=∑j=1q∏i=1dVi,j​(xi),\displaystyle V(x)=\sum_{j=1}^{q}\prod_{i=1}^{d}V_{i,j}(x_{i}), (3.17)

where Vi,j​(xi)∈L2​(Ωi)V_{i,j}(x_{i})\in L^{2}(\Omega_{i}). Then the equivalent variational form of the eigenvalue problem (3.16) can be defined as follows: Find (λ,u)∈ℝ×H01​(Ω)(\lambda,u)\in\mathbb{R}\times H_{0}^{1}(\Omega) such that

a⁡(u,v)=λ​b​(u,v),∀v∈H01​(Ω),\displaystyle a(u,v)=\lambda b(u,v),\ \ \ \ \forall v\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega), (3.18)

where the bilinear forms a⁡(⋅,⋅)a(\cdot,\cdot) and b⁡(⋅,⋅)b(\cdot,\cdot) are defined as follows

a⁡(u,v)=∫Ω(∇u⋅∇v+V​u​v)​𝑑Ω,b⁡(u,v)=∫Ωu​v​𝑑Ω.\displaystyle a(u,v)=\int_{\Omega}(\nabla u\cdot\nabla v+Vuv)d\Omega,\ \ \ \ \ \ b(u,v)=\int_{\Omega}uvd\Omega. (3.19)

Due to the definition of kk TNNs (3.9) and (3.17), entries of the matrix 𝒜\mathcal{A} in the loss function (3.10) have following expansions

𝒜m​n\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{mn} =\displaystyle= a⁡(Ψm​(x,Θm),Ψn​(x,Θn))\displaystyle a\big(\Psi_{m}(x;\Theta_{m}),\Psi_{n}(x;\Theta_{n})\big) (3.20)
=\displaystyle= ∑s=1d∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,m​cℓ,n​∏i≠sd∫Ωiϕi,j,m​(xi,θi,m)​ϕi,ℓ,n​(xi,θi,n)​d​xi\displaystyle\sum_{s=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i\neq s}^{d}\int_{\Omega_{i}}\phi_{i,j,m}(x_{i};\theta_{i,m})\phi_{i,\ell,n}(x_{i};\theta_{i,n})dx_{i}
⋅∫Ωs∂ϕs,j,m∂xs​(xs,θs,m)​∂ϕs,ℓ,n∂xs​(xs,θs,n)​d​xs\displaystyle\ \ \ \ \ \cdot\int_{\Omega_{s}}\frac{\partial\phi_{s,j,m}}{\partial x_{s}}(x_{s};\theta_{s,m})\frac{\partial\phi_{s,\ell,n}}{\partial x_{s}}(x_{s};\theta_{s,n})dx_{s}
+∑s=1q∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,mcℓ,n∏i=1d∫ΩiVi,s(xi)ϕi,j,m(xi;θi,m)ϕi,ℓ,m(xi;θi,n)dxi,\displaystyle\ \ +\sum_{s=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i=1}^{d}\int_{\Omega_{i}}V_{i,s}(x_{i})\phi_{i,j,m}(x_{i};\theta_{i,m})\phi_{i,\ell,m}(x_{i};\theta_{i,n})dx_{i},

and entries of the matrix ℬ\mathcal{B} can be expanded as follows

ℬm​n\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{mn} =\displaystyle= b⁡(Ψm​(x,Θm),Ψn​(x,Θn))\displaystyle b\big(\Psi_{m}(x;\Theta_{m}),\Psi_{n}(x;\Theta_{n})\big) (3.21)
=\displaystyle= ∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,m​cℓ,n​∏i=1d∫Ωiϕi,j,m​(xi,θi,m)​ϕi,ℓ,n​(xi,θi,n)​d​xi.\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i=1}^{d}\int_{\Omega_{i}}\phi_{i,j,m}(x_{i};\theta_{i,m})\phi_{i,\ell,n}(x_{i};\theta_{i,n})dx_{i}.

Since only one-dimensional integrations are involved in (3.20) and (3.21), there is no need to use the Monte Carlo procedure to do these high dimensional integrations. In order to guarantee the high accuracy of the high dimensional integrations included in the loss functions, we should use the high order one dimensional quadrature scheme, such as Gauss-type rules [10], for the integrations in (3.20) and (3.21).

3.2.1 Legendre-Gauss quadrature scheme for bounded domain

Without loss of generality, we decompose each Ωi\Omega_{i} into MiM_{i} equal subintervals with length hi=|Ωi|/Mih_{i}=|\Omega_{i}|/M_{i} and choose NiN_{i} Legendre-Gauss points in each subinterval. Denote the total quadrature points and corresponding weights as follows

{xi(ni)}ni=1Mi​Ni,{wi(ni)}ni=1Mi​Ni,i=1,2,⋯,d,\displaystyle\left\{x_{i}^{(n_{i})}\right\}_{n_{i}=1}^{M_{i}N_{i}},\ \ \ \left\{w_{i}^{(n_{i})}\right\}_{n_{i}=1}^{M_{i}N_{i}},\ \ \ i=1,2,\cdots,d, (3.22)

and define N=max⁡{N1,⋯,Nd}N=\max\{N_{1},\cdots,N_{d}\}, N¯=min⁡{N1,⋯,Nd}\underline{N}=\min\{N_{1},\cdots,N_{d}\}, M=max⁡{M1,⋯,Md}M=\max\{M_{1},\cdots,M_{d}\} and M¯=min⁡{M1,⋯,Md}\underline{M}=\min\{M_{1},\cdots,M_{d}\}. Then using the quadrature scheme (3.22), entries of the matrix 𝒜\mathcal{A} defined by (3.20) have the following numerical format

𝒜m​n=a⁡(Ψm​(x,Θm),Ψn​(x,Θn))\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{mn}=a\big(\Psi_{m}(x;\Theta_{m}),\Psi_{n}(x;\Theta_{n})\big)
≈∑s=1d∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,m​cℓ,n​∏i≠sd∑ni=1Mi​Niwi(ni)​ϕi,j,m​(xi(ni),θi,m)​ϕi,ℓ,n​(xi(ni),θi,n)\displaystyle\approx\sum_{s=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i\neq s}^{d}\sum_{n_{i}=1}^{M_{i}N_{i}}w_{i}^{(n_{i})}\phi_{i,j,m}(x_{i}^{(n_{i})};\theta_{i,m})\phi_{i,\ell,n}(x_{i}^{(n_{i})};\theta_{i,n})
⋅∑ns=1Ms​Nsws(ns)​∂ϕs,j,m∂xs​(xs(ns),θs,m)​∂ϕs,ℓ,n∂xs​(xs(ns),θs,n)\displaystyle\cdot\sum_{n_{s}=1}^{M_{s}N_{s}}w_{s}^{(n_{s})}\frac{\partial\phi_{s,j,m}}{\partial x_{s}}(x_{s}^{(n_{s})};\theta_{s,m})\frac{\partial\phi_{s,\ell,n}}{\partial x_{s}}(x_{s}^{(n_{s})};\theta_{s,n})
+∑s=1q∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,mcℓ,n∏i=1d∑ni=1Mi​Niwi(ni)Vi,s(xi(ni))ϕi,j,m(xi(ni);θi,m)ϕi,ℓ,m(xi(ni);θi,n),\displaystyle+\sum_{s=1}^{q}\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{n_{i}=1}^{M_{i}N_{i}}w_{i}^{(n_{i})}V_{i,s}(x_{i}^{(n_{i})})\phi_{i,j,m}(x_{i}^{(n_{i})};\theta_{i,m})\phi_{i,\ell,m}(x_{i}^{(n_{i})};\theta_{i,n}), (3.23)

and entries of the matrix ℬ\mathcal{B} defined by (3.21) can be computed as follows

ℬm​n\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{mn} =\displaystyle= b⁡(Ψm​(x,Θm),Ψn​(x,Θn))\displaystyle b\big(\Psi_{m}(x;\Theta_{m}),\Psi_{n}(x;\Theta_{n})\big) (3.24)
≈\displaystyle\approx ∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,m​cℓ,n​∏i=1d∑ni=1Mi​Niwi(ni)​ϕi,j,m​(xi(ni),θi,m)​ϕi,ℓ,n​(xi(ni),θi,n).\displaystyle\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{n_{i}=1}^{M_{i}N_{i}}w_{i}^{(n_{i})}\phi_{i,j,m}(x_{i}^{(n_{i})};\theta_{i,m})\phi_{i,\ell,n}(x_{i}^{(n_{i})};\theta_{i,n}).

Then the complete TNN-based algorithm for computing the first kk eigenpairs can be summarized in Algorithm 1.

It is worth mentioning that the quadrature schemes (3.23) and (3.24) which use 11-dimensional Mi​NiM_{i}N_{i} quadrature points in each dimension are actually equivalent to implementing the following dd-dimensional full tensor quadrature scheme

𝒜m​n\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{mn} ≈\displaystyle\approx ∑n∈𝒩w(n)∇Ψm(x(n);Θm)⋅∇Ψn(x(n);Θn)\displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}w^{(n)}\nabla\Psi_{m}(x^{(n)};\Theta_{m})\cdot\nabla\Psi_{n}(x^{(n)};\Theta_{n})
+∑n∈𝒩w(n)V(x(n))Ψm(x(n);Θm)Ψn(x(n);Θn),\displaystyle+\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}w^{(n)}V(x^{(n)})\Psi_{m}(x^{(n)};\Theta_{m})\Psi_{n}(x^{(n)};\Theta_{n}),
ℬm​n\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{mn} ≈\displaystyle\approx ∑n∈𝒩w(n)​Ψm​(x(n),Θm)​Ψn​(x(n),Θn),\displaystyle\sum_{n\in\mathcal{N}}w^{(n)}\Psi_{m}(x^{(n)};\Theta_{m})\Psi_{n}(x^{(n)};\Theta_{n}), (3.25)

where dd-dimensional quadrature points and weights are defined as follows

{x(n)}n∈𝒩={{x1(n1)}n1=1M1​N1×{x2(n2)}n2=1M2​N2×⋯×{xd(nd)}nd=1Md​Nd},{w(n)}n∈𝒩={{w1(n1)}n1=1M1​N1×{w2(n2)}n2=1M2​N2×⋯,×{wd(nd)}nd=1Md​Nd}.\displaystyle\left.\begin{array}[]{rcl}\Big\{x^{(n)}\Big\}_{n\in\mathcal{N}}&=&\left\{\left\{x_{1}^{(n_{1})}\right\}_{n_{1}=1}^{M_{1}N_{1}}\times\ \left\{x_{2}^{(n_{2})}\right\}_{n_{2}=1}^{M_{2}N_{2}}\times\ \cdots\times\ \left\{x_{d}^{(n_{d})}\right\}_{n_{d}=1}^{M_{d}N_{d}}\right\},\\ \Big\{w^{(n)}\Big\}_{n\in\mathcal{N}}&=&\left\{\left\{w_{1}^{(n_{1})}\right\}_{n_{1}=1}^{M_{1}N_{1}}\times\left\{w_{2}^{(n_{2})}\right\}_{n_{2}=1}^{M_{2}N_{2}}\times\cdots,\times\left\{w_{d}^{(n_{d})}\right\}_{n_{d}=1}^{M_{d}N_{d}}\right\}.\end{array}\right.

The quadrature points (3.2.1) for general dd-dimensional integrand has accuracy 𝒪⁡(h2​N¯/(2​N¯)!)\mathcal{O}(h^{2\underline{N}}/(2\underline{N})!) but 𝒩\mathcal{N} has 𝒪⁡(Md​Nd)\mathcal{O}(M^{d}N^{d}) elements. This becomes too large for d≫1d\gg 1 and makes the approximation of integration intractable. Thanks to TNN having the low-rank tensor type structure, using the full tensor quadrature scheme for the inner product of two TNNs has the splitting schemes (3.23) and (3.24). In quadrature schemes (3.23) and (3.24), assembling matrices 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B} costs only 𝒪⁡(d2​p2​M​N+d​p2​q​M​N)\mathcal{O}(d^{2}p^{2}MN+dp^{2}qMN) and 𝒪⁡(d​p2​M​N)\mathcal{O}(dp^{2}MN) operations, respectively. Furthermore, due to the equivalence of using full tensor quadrature points (3.2.1), quadrature schemes (3.23) and (3.24) also have accuracy 𝒪⁡(h2​N¯/(2​N¯)!)\mathcal{O}(h^{2\underline{N}}/(2\underline{N})!). This means the TNN-based method proposed in this paper overcomes the “curse of dimensionality” in the sense of numerical integration.

For generality, in the next two sections, we will also introduce the integration of TNN on unbounded domains. The corresponding complexity analysis will be omitted since they are similar to that in this section.

3.2.2 Hermite-Gauss quadrature scheme for the whole line

For case Ωi=(−∞,+∞)\Omega_{i}=(-\infty,+\infty), we use Hermite-Gauss quadrature to assemble matrix 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}. Hermite-Gauss quadrature scheme satisfies following property.

Lemma 1.

[31, Theorem 7.3] Let {x(k)}k=0N\{x^{(k)}\}_{k=0}^{N} be the zeros of the (N+1)(N+1)-th order Hermite polynomial HN+1​(x)H_{N+1}(x), and let {w(k)}k=1N\{w^{(k)}\}_{k=1}^{N} be given by

w(k)=π​2N​N!(N+1)​HN2​(x(k)), 0≤k≤N.\displaystyle w^{(k)}=\frac{\sqrt{\pi}2^{N}N!}{(N+1)H_{N}^{2}(x^{(k)})},\ \ \ 0\leq k\leq N. (3.29)

Then we have

∫−∞+∞p⁡(x)​e−x2​𝑑x=∑k=0Np⁡(x(k))​w(k),∀p∈P2​N+1,\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}p(x)e^{-x^{2}}dx=\sum_{k=0}^{N}p(x^{(k)})w^{(k)},\ \ \ \forall p\in P_{2N+1}, (3.30)

where P2​N+1P_{2N+1} denotes the set of polynomial functions of degree less than 2​N+12N+1.

For using Hermite-Gauss quadrature, the ii-th subnetwork of ℓ\ell-th TNN is defined as follows

Φi,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ)\displaystyle\Phi_{i,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}) =\displaystyle= (ϕi,1,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ),ϕi,2,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ),⋯,ϕi,p,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ))\displaystyle\big(\phi_{i,1,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\phi_{i,2,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\cdots,\phi_{i,p,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\big)
=\displaystyle= e−βi2​xi22​(φi,1,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),φi,2,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),⋯,φi,p,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)),\displaystyle e^{-\frac{\beta_{i}^{2}x_{i}^{2}}{2}}\big(\varphi_{i,1,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\varphi_{i,2,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\cdots,\varphi_{i,p,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\big),

where βi\beta_{i} is trainable parameter and φi,ℓ=(φi,1,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),φi,2,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),⋯,φi,p,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ))\varphi_{i,\ell}=\big(\varphi_{i,1,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\varphi_{i,2,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\cdots,\varphi_{i,p,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\big) is a fully-connected neural network which maps ℝ\mathbb{R} to ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}. Then the ℓ\ell-th TNN can be written as

Ψℓ​(x,Θℓ)=∑j=1pcj,ℓ​∏i=1de−βi2​xi22​φ^i,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),\displaystyle\Psi_{\ell}(x;\Theta_{\ell})=\sum_{j=1}^{p}c_{j,\ell}\prod_{i=1}^{d}e^{-\frac{\beta_{i}^{2}x_{i}^{2}}{2}}\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}), (3.31)

where φ^i,j,ℓ\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,\ell} satisfies normalization property ‖e−βi2​xi22​φ^i,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)‖L2​(Ωi)=1\|e^{-\frac{\beta_{i}^{2}x_{i}^{2}}{2}}\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{i})}=1 and is defined as follows

φ^i,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)=φi,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)‖e−βi2​xi22​φi,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)‖L2​(Ωi).\displaystyle\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})=\frac{\varphi_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})}{\Big\|e^{-\frac{\beta_{i}^{2}x_{i}^{2}}{2}}\varphi_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\Big\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{i})}}. (3.32)

For i=1,⋯,di=1,\cdots,d, let {zi(ki)}ki=1Ni\{z_{i}^{(k_{i})}\}_{k_{i}=1}^{N_{i}} and {wi(ki)}ki=1Ni\{w_{i}^{(k_{i})}\}_{k_{i}=1}^{N_{i}} be the Hermite-Gauss quadrature points and weights, respectively. Under coordinate transformation zi=βi​xiz_{i}=\beta_{i}x_{i}, using the quadrature scheme (3.30), entries of the matrix 𝒜\mathcal{A} defined by (3.20) have the following numerical format

𝒜m​n=∑i=1d∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,m​cℓ,n​∏i≠sd1βi​∑ki=1Niφ^i,j,m​(zi(ki),θi,m)​φ^i,ℓ,n​(zi(ki),θi,n)​wi(ki)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{mn}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i\neq s}^{d}\frac{1}{\beta_{i}}\sum_{k_{i}=1}^{N_{i}}\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,m}(z_{i}^{(k_{i})};\theta_{i,m})\widehat{\varphi}_{i,\ell,n}(z_{i}^{(k_{i})};\theta_{i,n})w_{i}^{(k_{i})}
⋅1βs​∑ksNs(φ^s,j,m′​(zs(ks),θs,m)−βs​φ^s,j,m​(zs(ks),θs,m))\displaystyle\cdot\frac{1}{\beta_{s}}\sum_{k_{s}}^{N_{s}}\big(\widehat{\varphi}_{s,j,m}^{\prime}(z_{s}^{(k_{s})};\theta_{s,m})-\beta_{s}\widehat{\varphi}_{s,j,m}(z_{s}^{(k_{s})};\theta_{s,m})\big)

(3.33)

And entries of the matrix ℬ\mathcal{B} defined by (3.21) have the following numerical format

ℬm​n=∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,m​cℓ,n​∏i=1d1βi​∑ki=1Niφ^i,j,m​(zi(ki),θi,m)​φ^i,ℓ,n​(zi(ki),θi,n)​wi(ki).\displaystyle\mathcal{B}_{mn}=\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i=1}^{d}\frac{1}{\beta_{i}}\sum_{k_{i}=1}^{N_{i}}\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,m}(z_{i}^{(k_{i})};\theta_{i,m})\widehat{\varphi}_{i,\ell,n}(z_{i}^{(k_{i})};\theta_{i,n})w_{i}^{(k_{i})}. (3.34)

3.2.3 Laguerre-Gauss quadrature scheme for the half line

For case Ωi=(0,+∞)\Omega_{i}=(0,+\infty), we use Laguerre-Gauss quadrature to assemble matrices 𝒜\mathcal{A} and ℬ\mathcal{B}. Laguerre-Gauss quadrature satisfies the following theorem

Lemma 2.

[31, Theorem 7.1] Let {x(k)}k=0N\{x^{(k)}\}_{k=0}^{N} be the zeros of the (N+1)(N+1)-th order Laguerre polynomial ℒN+1​(x)\mathcal{L}_{N+1}(x), and let {w(k)}k=0N\{w^{(k)}\}_{k=0}^{N} be given by

w(k)=Γ⁡(N+1)(N+1)​(N+1)!​x(k)[ℒN​(x(k))]2, 0≤0≤N.\displaystyle w^{(k)}=\frac{\Gamma(N+1)}{(N+1)(N+1)!}\frac{x^{(k)}}{\big[\mathcal{L}_{N}(x^{(k)})\big]^{2}},\ \ \ 0\leq 0\leq N. (3.35)

Then we have

∫−∞+∞p⁡(x)​e−x​𝑑x=∑k=0Np⁡(x(k))​w(k),∀p∈P2​N+1,\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{+\infty}p(x)e^{-x}dx=\sum_{k=0}^{N}p(x^{(k)})w^{(k)},\ \ \ \forall p\in P_{2N+1}, (3.36)

where P2​N+1P_{2N+1} denotes the set of polynomial functions of degree less than 2​N+12N+1.

For using Laguerre-Gauss quadrature, the ii-th subnetwork of the ℓ\ell-th TNN is defined as follows

Φi,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ)\displaystyle\Phi_{i,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}) =\displaystyle= (ϕi,1,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ),ϕi,2,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ),⋯,ϕi,p,ℓ​(xi,θi,ℓ))\displaystyle\big(\phi_{i,1,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\phi_{i,2,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\cdots,\phi_{i,p,\ell}(x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\big)
=\displaystyle= e−βi​xi2​(φi,1,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),φi,2,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),⋯,φi,p,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)),\displaystyle e^{-\frac{\beta_{i}x_{i}}{2}}\big(\varphi_{i,1,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\varphi_{i,2,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\cdots,\varphi_{i,p,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\big),

where βi\beta_{i} is trainable parameter and φi,ℓ=(φi,1,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),φi,2,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),⋯,φi,p,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ))\varphi_{i,\ell}=\big(\varphi_{i,1,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\varphi_{i,2,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}),\cdots,\varphi_{i,p,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\big) is a fully-connected neural network which maps ℝ\mathbb{R} to ℝp\mathbb{R}^{p}. Then the ℓ\ell-th TNN can be written as

Ψℓ​(x,Θℓ)=∑j=1pcj,ℓ​∏i=1de−βi​xi2​φ^i,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ),\displaystyle\Psi_{\ell}(x;\Theta_{\ell})=\sum_{j=1}^{p}c_{j,\ell}\prod_{i=1}^{d}e^{-\frac{\beta_{i}x_{i}}{2}}\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell}), (3.37)

where φ^i,j,ℓ\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,\ell} satisfies normalization property ‖e−βi​xi2​φ^i,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)‖L2​(Ωi)=1\|e^{-\frac{\beta_{i}x_{i}}{2}}\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{i})}=1 and is defined as follows

φ^i,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)=φi,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)‖e−βi​xi2​φi,j,ℓ​(βi​xi,θi,ℓ)‖L2​(Ωi).\displaystyle\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})=\frac{\varphi_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})}{\Big\|e^{-\frac{\beta_{i}x_{i}}{2}}\varphi_{i,j,\ell}(\beta_{i}x_{i};\theta_{i,\ell})\Big\|_{L^{2}(\Omega_{i})}}. (3.38)

𝒜m​n=∑i=1d∑j=1pm∑ℓ=1pncj,m​cℓ,n​∏i≠sd1βi​∑ki=1Niφ^i,j,m​(zi(ki),θi,m)​φ^i,ℓ,n​(zi(ki),θi,n)​wi(ki)\displaystyle\mathcal{A}_{mn}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\sum_{j=1}^{p_{m}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{p_{n}}c_{j,m}c_{\ell,n}\prod_{i\neq s}^{d}\frac{1}{\beta_{i}}\sum_{k_{i}=1}^{N_{i}}\widehat{\varphi}_{i,j,m}(z_{i}^{(k_{i})};\theta_{i,m})\widehat{\varphi}_{i,\ell,n}(z_{i}^{(k_{i})};\theta_{i,n})w_{i}^{(k_{i})}

4 Numerical examples

In this section, we provide several examples to investigate the performance of the TNN-based eigensolver proposed in this paper. To show the convergence behavior and accuracy of our method, we define the relative errors for the approximated eigenvalues λ^ℓ\widehat{\lambda}_{\ell} and eigenfunctions 𝐲ℓ\mathbf{y}_{\ell} as follows

errλ,ℓ:=|λ^ℓ−λℓ||λℓ|,errL2,ℓ:=‖uℓ−𝒬ℓ​uℓ‖L2​(Ω)‖uℓ‖L2​(Ω),errH1,ℓ:=|uℓ−𝒫ℓ​uℓ|H1​(Ω)|uℓ|H1​(Ω),ℓ=1,⋯,k,\displaystyle{\rm err}_{\lambda,\ell}:=\frac{|\widehat{\lambda}_{\ell}-\lambda_{\ell}|}{|\lambda_{\ell}|},\ {\rm err}_{L^{2},\ell}:=\frac{\|u_{\ell}-\mathcal{Q}_{\ell}u_{\ell}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}}{\|u_{\ell}\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}},\ {\rm err}_{H^{1},\ell}:=\frac{\left|u_{\ell}-\mathcal{P}_{\ell}u_{\ell}\right|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}}{\left|u_{\ell}\right|_{H^{1}(\Omega)}},\ \ell=1,\cdots,k, (4.1)

where λℓ\lambda_{\ell} and uℓu_{\ell} are reference eigenvalues and eigenfunctions. In the first two examples, the reference eigenpairs are obtained by high order finite element methods on the meshes with a sufficiently small mesh size. As for the harmonic oscillator problems, the exact eigenpairs are chosen as references. In (4.1), 𝒫ℓ:H01​(Ω)→Mℓ\mathcal{P}_{\ell}:H_{0}^{1}(\Omega)\rightarrow M_{\ell} and 𝒬:H01​(Ω)→Mℓ\mathcal{Q}:H_{0}^{1}(\Omega)\rightarrow M_{\ell} denote L2​(Ω)L^{2}(\Omega) projection operator and H1​(Ω)H^{1}(\Omega) projection operator, respectively, to the approximate eigenspace corresponding to the eigenvalue λℓ\lambda_{\ell}. These two projection operators are defined as follows

⟨𝒫ℓ​u,v⟩L2\displaystyle\left\langle\mathcal{P}_{\ell}u,v\right\rangle_{L^{2}} =\displaystyle= ⟨u,v⟩L2:=∫Ωu​v​𝑑x,∀v∈Mℓfor​u∈H01​(Ω),\displaystyle\left\langle u,v\right\rangle_{L^{2}}:=\int_{\Omega}uvdx,\ \ \ \forall v\in M_{\ell}\ \ {\rm for}\ u\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega), (4.2)
⟨𝒬ℓ​u,v⟩H1\displaystyle\left\langle\mathcal{Q}_{\ell}u,v\right\rangle_{H^{1}} =\displaystyle= ⟨u,v⟩H1:=∫Ω∇u⋅∇v​𝑑x,∀v∈Mℓfor​u∈H01​(Ω).\displaystyle\left\langle u,v\right\rangle_{H^{1}}:=\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot\nabla vdx,\ \ \ \forall v\in M_{\ell}\ \ {\rm for}\ u\in H_{0}^{1}(\Omega). (4.3)

In implementation, we use the quadrature scheme similar to that in (3.23) and (3.24), (3.33) and (3.34), (3.39) and (3.40), to compute errL2,ℓ{\rm err}_{L^{2},\ell} and errH1,ℓ{\rm err}_{H^{1},\ell} with the same tensor product quadrature points and weights as computing the loss functions if the reference solution uℓ​(x)u_{\ell}(x) has a low-rank representation, otherwise we only report errλ,ℓ{\rm err}_{\lambda,\ell}. With the help of Theorem 2 in [32], the high efficiency and accuracy for computing errL2,ℓ{\rm err}_{L^{2},\ell} and errH1,ℓ{\rm err}_{H^{1},\ell} can be guaranteed.

4.1 Infinitesimal generators of metastable diffusion processes

In this subsection, we study the eigenvalue problem from [36] associated with the operator

ℒd=∇Vd⋅∇−Δ.\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{d}=\nabla V_{d}\cdot\nabla-\Delta. (4.4)

The potential functions Vd:ℝd→ℝV_{d}:\mathbb{R}^{d}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} for d=2,50,100d=2,50,100 are defined as follows

Vd​(x)=V⁡(θ)+2​(r−1)2+5​e−5​r2+5​∑i=3dxi2,∀x=(x1,x2,⋯,xd)∈ℝd,\displaystyle V_{d}(x)=V(\theta)+2(r-1)^{2}+5e^{-5r^{2}}+5\sum_{i=3}^{d}x_{i}^{2},\ \ \ \forall x=(x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{d})\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, (4.5)

where (r,θ)∈[0,+∞)×[−π,π)(r,\theta)\in[0,+\infty)\times[-\pi,\pi) denotes the polar coordinates which relate to the first two dimensional Eucild space (x1,x2)∈ℝ2(x_{1},x_{2})\in\mathbb{R}^{2} by

x1=r​cos⁡θ,x2=r​sin⁡θ,\displaystyle x_{1}=r\cos\theta,\ \ \ x_{2}=r\sin\theta, (4.6)

and V:[−π,π)→ℝV:[-\pi,\pi)\rightarrow\mathbb{R} is a double-well potential function which is defined as follows

V(θ)={[1−(3​θπ+1)2]2,θ∈[−π,−π3),15​(3−2​cos⁡(3​θ)),θ∈[−π3,π3),[1−(3​θπ−1)2]2,θ∈[π3,π).\displaystyle V(\theta)=\left\{\begin{aligned} &\left[1-\left(\frac{3\theta}{\pi}+1\right)^{2}\right]^{2},&\ \ \ &\theta\in\left[-\pi,-\frac{\pi}{3}\right),\\ &\frac{1}{5}\left(3-2\cos(3\theta)\right),&\ \ \ &\theta\in\left[-\frac{\pi}{3},\frac{\pi}{3}\right),\\ &\left[1-\left(\frac{3\theta}{\pi}-1\right)^{2}\right]^{2},&\ \ \ &\theta\in\left[\frac{\pi}{3},\pi\right).\end{aligned}\right. (4.7)

The reference eigenvalue for d=2d=2 is obtained by using the third order conforming finite element method with the mesh size h=31024​2h=\frac{3}{1024}\sqrt{2} on the domain [−3,3]2⊂ℝ2[-3,3]^{2}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2}. Here we use the open parallel finite element package OpenPFEM [34] to do the discretization and then using Krylovschur method from SLEPc [16] to solve the corresponding algebraic eigenvalue problem 11 1 We express our thanks to Yangfei Liao for this computation. In this way, we obtain the first three eigenvalues

λ1=0.21881493133369,λ2=0.76371970025476,λ3=2.79019347384363,\lambda_{1}=0.21881493133369,\ \ \ \lambda_{2}=0.76371970025476,\ \ \ \lambda_{3}=2.79019347384363,

as the reference values for our numerical investigation. The corresponding eigenfunctions are shown in the first column of Figure 2.

In implementation, we use 33 TNNs to learn the lowest 33 eigenvalues. For d=2,50,100d=2,50,100 cases, each TNN has depth 3 and width 20 and the rank is chosen to be p=10p=10. The Adam optimizer is employed with a learning rate 0.003. We use the Adam optimizer in the first 100000 steps and then the LBFGS in the subsequent 10000 steps. The final eigenvalue approximations are represented in Table 1 and the corresponding eigenfunction approximations are shown in Figure 2, where we can find the proposed method has obviously better accuracy than that in [36].

4.2 Harmonic oscillator problems

In this subsection, we consider the Schrödinger equation associated with the dd-dimensional harmonic oscillator and the corresponding Hamiltonian operator reads as

H=−12∑i=1d∇i2+12xTAx,\displaystyle H=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\nabla_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}x^{T}Ax, (4.8)

where x=(x1,x2,⋯,xd)Tx=(x_{1},x_{2},\cdots,x_{d})^{T}, A=(ai​j)d×d∈ℝd×dA=(a_{ij})_{d\times d}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} is a symmetric positive definite matrix.

The exact wavefunctions and the corresponding energy (i.e. eigenvalue) of different states can be obtained with the similar way in [4]. According to the property of the symmetric positive definite matrix, there exists an orthogonal matrix Q=(qi​j)d×d∈ℝd×dQ=(q_{ij})_{d\times d}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d} such that

QT​A​Q=diag⁡{μ1,μ2,⋯,μd},\displaystyle Q^{T}AQ={\rm diag}\big\{\mu_{1},\mu_{2},\cdots,\mu_{d}\big\}, (4.9)

where μj\mu_{j} and 𝐪j=(q1​j,q2​j,⋯,qd​j)T\mathbf{q}_{j}=(q_{1j},q_{2j},\cdots,q_{dj})^{T}, j=1,2,⋯,dj=1,2,\cdots,d are eigenvalues and corresponding normalized eigenvectors of the matrix AA. Then under the rotation transformation y=QT​xy=Q^{T}x, the Hamiltonian operator (4.8) in the coordinate system (y1,y2,⋯,yd)(y_{1},y_{2},\cdots,y_{d}) can be written as the following decoupled harmonic form

H=−12∑i=1d∇i2+12∑i=1dμiyi2.\displaystyle H=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\nabla_{i}^{2}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{d}\mu_{i}y_{i}^{2}. (4.10)

Then the exact wavefunction of state (n1,n2,⋯,nd)(n_{1},n_{2},\cdots,n_{d}) can be immediately obtained as follows

Ψn1,n2,⋯,nd(y1,y2,⋯,yd)=∏i=1dℋni(μi1/4yi)e−μi1/2yi2/2,\displaystyle\Psi_{n_{1},n_{2},\cdots,n_{d}}(y_{1},y_{2},\cdots,y_{d})=\prod_{i=1}^{d}\mathcal{H}_{n_{i}}(\mu_{i}^{1/4}y_{i})e^{-\mu_{i}^{1/2}y_{i}^{2}/2}, (4.11)

and the corresponding exact energy is

En1,n2,⋯,nd=∑i=1d(12+ni)​μi1/2,\displaystyle E_{n_{1},n_{2},\cdots,n_{d}}=\sum_{i=1}^{d}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+n_{i}\Big)\mu_{i}^{1/2}, (4.12)

where yi=∑j=1dqi​j​xjy_{i}=\sum_{j=1}^{d}q_{ij}x_{j} and ℋn\mathcal{H}_{n} is physicists’ Hermite polynomials [1].

In all three examples of this subsection, we adopt the same parameters ai​ja_{ij} as in [25] and calculate the lowest 1616 energy states as [25] done. The aim here is to demonstrate the performance of the proposed approach through these comparisons.

4.2.1 Two-dimensional harmonic oscillator

We first examine a simple case of the two-dimensional harmonic oscillator problem

−12​(∇12+∇22)​Ψ+12​(x12+x22)​Ψ=E​Ψ.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\nabla_{1}^{2}+\nabla_{2}^{2}\Big)\Psi+\frac{1}{2}(x_{1}^{2}+x_{2}^{2})\Psi=E\Psi. (4.13)

Since the problem is essentially decoupled, the exact eigenfunction has low-rank representation in coordinate (x1,x2)(x_{1},x_{2}) as follows

Ψn1,n2=ℋn1(x1)e−x12/2ℋn2(x2)e−x22/2.\displaystyle\Psi_{n_{1},n_{2}}=\mathcal{H}_{n_{1}}(x_{1})e^{-x_{1}^{2}/2}\mathcal{H}_{n_{2}}(x_{2})e^{-x_{2}^{2}/2}. (4.14)

The corresponding exact energy is

En1,n2=(12+n1)+(12+n2).\displaystyle E_{n_{1},n_{2}}=\Big(\frac{1}{2}+n_{1}\Big)+\Big(\frac{1}{2}+n_{2}\Big). (4.15)

We use 1616 TNNs to learn the lowest 1616 energy states and each subnetwork of a single TNN with depth 33 and width 5050, and p=20p=20. The Adam optimizer is employed with a learning rate 0.001 in the first 500000 epochs and then the L-BFGS in the subsequent 10000 steps to produce the final result. The Hermite-Gauss quadrature scheme with 9999 points are adopted in each dimension.

The corresponding numerical results are shown in Table 2, where we can find the proposed TNN-based machine learning method has obvious better accuracy than that in [25], where the accuracy is 1.01.0e-22 by the Monte-Carlo based machine learning methods.

4.2.2 Two-dimensional coupled harmonic oscillator

Since TNN-based methods carry out operations separately in each dimension, it is not unexpected that our method has an impressive performance in the completely decoupled case. To show the generalities of TNN-based machine learning method, the next two examples are to compute the multi-states of operators with coupled oscillators.

First, we consider the following two-dimensional eigenvalue problem of the operator with coupled harmonic oscillator

−12​(∇12+∇22)​Ψ+12​(a11​x12+2​a12​x1​x2+a22​x22)​Ψ=E​Ψ.\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\Big(\nabla_{1}^{2}+\nabla_{2}^{2}\Big)\Psi+\frac{1}{2}(a_{11}x_{1}^{2}+2a_{12}x_{1}x_{2}+a_{22}x_{2}^{2})\Psi=E\Psi. (4.16)

The coefficients a11,a12,a22a_{11},a_{12},a_{22} are chosen as in [25]. Since in [25] the coefficients are rounded to four decimal places, we use rounded values as exact coefficients, that is, a11=0.8851a_{11}=0.8851, a12=−0.1382a_{12}=-0.1382, a22=1.1933a_{22}=1.1933. The exact eigenfunction has the following representation in coordinate (y1,y2)(y_{1},y_{2})

Ψn1,n2(y1,y2)=ℋn1(μ11/4y1)e−μ11/2y12/2⋅ℋn2(μ21/4y2)e−μ21/2y22/2,\displaystyle\Psi_{n_{1},n_{2}}(y_{1},y_{2})=\mathcal{H}_{n_{1}}(\mu_{1}^{1/4}y_{1})e^{-\mu_{1}^{1/2}y_{1}^{2}/2}\cdot\mathcal{H}_{n_{2}}(\mu_{2}^{1/4}y_{2})e^{-\mu_{2}^{1/2}y_{2}^{2}/2}, (4.17)

where y1=−0.9339352418​x1−0.3574422527​x2y_{1}=-0.9339352418x_{1}-0.3574422527x_{2} and y2=0.3574422527​x1−0.9339352418y_{2}=0.3574422527x_{1}-0.9339352418, μ1=0.8322071257\mu_{1}=0.8322071257, μ2=1.2461928742\mu_{2}=1.2461928742, the two quantum numbers n1,n2n_{1},n_{2} take the values 0,1,2,⋯0,1,2,\cdots. The exact energy for the state (n1,n2)(n_{1},n_{2}) is

En1,n2=(12+n1)​μ11/2+(12+n2)​μ21/2.\displaystyle E_{n_{1},n_{2}}=\Big(\frac{1}{2}+n_{1}\Big)\mu_{1}^{1/2}+\Big(\frac{1}{2}+n_{2}\Big)\mu_{2}^{1/2}. (4.18)

We use 1616 TNNs to learn the lowest 1616 energy states. In each TNN, the rank is chosen to be p=20p=20, the subnetwork is built with depth 33 and width 5050. The Adam optimizer is employed with a learning rate 0.001. We use the Adam optimizer in the first 500000 steps and then the L-BFGS in the subsequent 10000 steps. In each direction, 9999 points Hermite-Gauss quadrature scheme are used to do the integration.

The corresponding numerical results are collected in Table 3, where we can find the proposed numerical method can also obtain the higher accuracy for the Schrödinger equation with coupled harmonic oscillator.

The corresponding approximate wavefunctions obtained by TNN-based machine learning method and the exact wavefunctions are shown in Figure 3, which implies that the approximate wavefunctions have very good accuracy even for the coupled harmonic oscillator.

4.2.3 Five-dimensional coupled harmonic oscillator

Then, we investigate the performance of the proposed method for the case of five-dimensional coupled harmonic oscillator. Here, the Hamiltonian operator is defined as (4.8) with the matrix AA being replaced with the following matrix

A=[1.058860420.013650340.091639450.119752900.056250130.013650341.096137420.108879300.074489740.074076520.091639450.108879301.009359130.055885430.089689560.119752900.074489740.055885431.176271290.060490450.056250130.074076520.089689560.060490450.94969417].\displaystyle A=\begin{bmatrix}1.05886042&0.01365034&0.09163945&0.11975290&0.05625013\\ 0.01365034&1.09613742&0.10887930&0.07448974&0.07407652\\ 0.09163945&0.10887930&1.00935913&0.05588543&0.08968956\\ 0.11975290&0.07448974&0.05588543&1.17627129&0.06049045\\ 0.05625013&0.07407652&0.08968956&0.06049045&0.94969417\end{bmatrix}. (4.19)

Then the exact energy is

En1,n2,⋯,n5=∑i=15(12+ni)​μi1/2,\displaystyle E_{n_{1},n_{2},\cdots,n_{5}}=\sum_{i=1}^{5}\Big(\frac{1}{2}+n_{i}\Big)\mu_{i}^{1/2}, (4.20)

where μ1=0.88021303\mu_{1}=0.88021303, μ2=0.90973982\mu_{2}=0.90973982, μ3=1.02312382\mu_{3}=1.02312382, μ4=1.10243017\mu_{4}=1.10243017, μ5=1.37481559\mu_{5}=1.37481559, each of the five quantum numbers nin_{i}, i=1,2,⋯,5i=1,2,\cdots,5 takes the values 0,1,2,⋯0,1,2,\cdots.

We use 1616 TNNs to learn the lowest 1616 energy states. A larger TNN structure than the 2-dimensional example is used, the rank is chosen to be p=50p=50, the subnetwork is built with depth 33 and width 100100. The Adam optimizer is employed with a learning rate 0.001 and epochs of 500000. Then the final result is given by the subsequent 10000 steps LBFGS. The same 99 points Hermite-Gauss quadrature scheme as that in the last two examples is sufficient to this example.

4.3 Energy states of hydrogen atom

In this section, we study energy states of hydrogen atom. The wave function Ψ⁡(x,y,z)\Psi(x,y,z) of the hydrogen atom satisfies the following Schrödinger equation

−12​Δ​Ψ−Ψ|𝐫|=E​Ψ,\displaystyle-\frac{1}{2}\Delta\Psi-\frac{\Psi}{|\mathbf{r}|}=E\Psi, (4.21)

where |𝐫|=(x2+y2+z2)1/2|\mathbf{r}|=(x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2})^{1/2}. The exact energy of the hydrogen atom are En=−12​n2E_{n}=-\frac{1}{2n^{2}} and there are n2n^{2} states consist with energy EnE_{n}.

In order to compute the singular integrals of the Column potential terms 1/|𝐫|1/|\mathbf{r}|, we adopt spherical coordinates (r,θ,φ)(r,\theta,\varphi) with density r2​sin⁡θr^{2}\sin\theta. Then the wave function Ψ⁡(𝐫)\Psi(\mathbf{r}) should be written as Ψ⁡(r,θ,φ)\Psi(r,\theta,\varphi). The Laplace Δ\Delta has following expression

Δ​Ψ\displaystyle\Delta\Psi =\displaystyle= ∂2Ψ∂r2+2r​∂Ψ∂r+1r2​∂2Ψ∂θ2+cos⁡θr2​sin⁡θ​∂Ψ∂θ+1r2​sin2⁡θ​∂2Ψ∂φ2\displaystyle\frac{\partial^{2}\Psi}{\partial r^{2}}+\frac{2}{r}\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial r}+\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial^{2}\Psi}{\partial\theta^{2}}+\frac{\cos\theta}{r^{2}\sin\theta}\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial\theta}+\frac{1}{r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}\frac{\partial^{2}\Psi}{\partial\varphi^{2}} (4.22)
=\displaystyle= 1r2​∂∂r​(r2​∂Ψ∂r)+1r2​sin⁡θ​∂∂θ​(sin⁡θ​∂Ψ∂θ)+1r2​sin2⁡θ​∂2Ψ∂φ2.\displaystyle\frac{1}{r^{2}}\frac{\partial}{\partial r}\left(r^{2}\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial r}\right)+\frac{1}{r^{2}\sin\theta}\frac{\partial}{\partial\theta}\left(\sin\theta\frac{\partial\Psi}{\partial\theta}\right)+\frac{1}{r^{2}\sin^{2}\theta}\frac{\partial^{2}\Psi}{\partial\varphi^{2}}.

The 9999 points Laguerre-Gauss quadrature is used in the direction rr and 1616 points Legendre-Gauss quadrature with subintervals length π64\frac{\pi}{64} in directions θ,φ\theta,\varphi. The TNN structure is defined as follows

Ψ⁡(r,θ,φ)=∑j=1pcj​ϕr,j​(β​r)​e−β​r2⋅ϕθ,j​(θ)⋅(ϕφ,j​(φ)​sin⁡(φ/2)+γj),\displaystyle\Psi(r,\theta,\varphi)=\sum_{j=1}^{p}c_{j}\phi_{r,j}(\beta r)e^{-\frac{\beta r}{2}}\cdot\phi_{\theta,j}(\theta)\cdot\big(\phi_{\varphi,j}(\varphi)\sin(\varphi/2)+\gamma_{j}\big), (4.23)

where ϕr=(ϕr,1,⋯,ϕr,p)\phi_{r}=(\phi_{r,1},\cdots,\phi_{r,p}), ϕθ=(ϕθ,1,⋯,ϕθ,p)\phi_{\theta}=(\phi_{\theta,1},\cdots,\phi_{\theta,p}) and ϕφ=(ϕφ,1,⋯,ϕφ,p)\phi_{\varphi}=(\phi_{\varphi,1},\cdots,\phi_{\varphi,p}) are three FNNs with depth 33 and width 5050, and p=20p=20. The activation function is selected as sin⁡(x)\sin(x). The trainable parameter γj\gamma_{j} is introduced to satisfy periodic boundary conditions Ψ⁡(r,θ,0)=Ψ⁡(r,θ,2​π)\Psi(r,\theta,0)=\Psi(r,\theta,2\pi).

In implement, we use 15 TNNs to learn the lowest 15 energy states, each TNN is defined as (4.23). The Adam optimizer is employed with a learning rate 0.0003 and epochs of 100000 and then the L-BFGS in the subsequent 10000 steps to produce the final result. Table 5 shows the final energy approximations and corresponding errors.

5 Conclusions

In this paper, based on the deep Ritz method, we design a type of TNN-based machine learning method to compute the leading multi-eigenpairs of high dimensional eigenvalue problems. The most important advantage of TNN is that the high dimensional integrations of TNN functions can be calculated with high accuracy and efficiency. Based on the high accuracy and efficiency of the high dimensional integration, we can build the corresponding machine learning method for solving high dimensional problems with the high accuracy. The presented numerical examples show that the proposed machine learning method in this paper can obtain obviously better accuracy than the Monte-Carlo-based machine learning methods.

In our numerical implementation, we also find that the accuracy and stability of the machine learning process should be paid more attention. These are necessary to get the final high accuracy for solving high dimensional problems by using machine learning methods.

Actually, the proposed TNN and the corresponding machine learning method can be extended to other high dimensional problems such as Schrödinger equations, Boltzmann equations, Fokker-Planck equations, stochastic equations, multiscale problems and so on. This means TNN-based machine learning method can bring more practical applications in physics, chemistry, biology, material science, engineering and so on. These will be our future work.
